Need to search first.I've written notes on all 21 verses, but there are real gaps. My search tool hit its usage limit early, so I couldn't open any full web pages. Everything below comes only from the excerpts the searches returned. That means I found nothing for the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Pentecostal, prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace sections, and v. 16 has no separate traditional comment. The labels "Reformed", "Methodist" and so on are my own descriptions of each writer, not the sources'.

On the biblehub.com "commentaries" pages, several older writers appear together. Where the excerpt didn't name the writer, I say "an older commentator on this page" rather than guess.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Ellicott thinks "rejoice in the Lord" may be a common way of saying "farewell in the Lord," so it works as closing good wishes. He links "the same things" and "safe" to the sharp warnings that follow, which repeat what Paul had taught before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm
- Matthew Henry: hearing the same truths often is good for us, because it refreshes our memory of important things. Wanting something new all the time is idle curiosity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_003.cfm
- Barnes: a Christian's main joy should be fellowship with the Lord, not riches or the world. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/philippians-3.html
- Deffinbaugh (on Precept Austin) calls this a turning-point verse, moving from humility to a warning about a heresy that denies the gospel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_31-6

**v. 2**
- Precept Austin: Paul says "watch out" three times, each as a present-tense command meaning "keep a watchful eye on" these men so as to avoid them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_31-6
- Guzik (Enduring Word): the "evil workers" both do evil and stress being right with God by works. The harsh language shows how much Paul cared about protecting the church from a works-based gospel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/
- Barclay: "dogs" was the name Jewish teachers used for the impure and for Gentiles, and Paul throws it back at them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/philippians-3.html
- Ellicott agrees with Chrysostom that Paul turns the name back on the Judaizers. He reads "concision" as mere cutting of the body, no longer the "seal" of the covenant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm
- Older commentators on biblehub: the "evil workers" were Judaizers who praised the law but sowed division. Another says these "dogs" stood outside the true fellowship of the saints. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/3-2.htm
- Constable explains a play on two Greek words: "circumcise" (the sacred sign) and "mutilate" (forbidden cutting of the body). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/philippians-3.html

**v. 3**
- Barnes: circumcision was always meant to picture turning away from the flesh. "The flesh" covers any advantage of birth, outward keeping of the law, or anything unaided human nature can do. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/philippians-3.html
- Ellicott: the better reading is "worship by the Spirit of God." The Greek word for "worship" was almost a technical term for Israel's worship. He links Colossians 2:11–12 and sees baptism in view there as the spiritual circumcision. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/philippians-3.html
- Constable: Paul uses three marks of the true people of God (Spirit-led worship, glorying in Christ, no confidence in human nature) to answer the three insults in v. 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/philippians-3.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, counts himself among the Gentiles here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/3-3.htm
- Precept Austin: the true circumcision is "made without hands," the Spirit's work on the heart. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_31-6

**v. 4**
- Matthew Henry: Paul didn't look down on these privileges because he lacked them. He had as much to boast of as any Jew. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_003.cfm
- Guzik: if anyone could claim to please God by keeping the law, it was Paul, who was better qualified than his opponents. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/

**v. 5**
- Ellicott:
  - "Eighth day" means he was born a Jew, not a convert.
  - "Hebrew of Hebrews" means a Jew who kept his fathers' language and customs.
  - "Pharisee" moves from privileges he inherited to the strict Judaism he chose.
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/philippians-3.html
- Matthew Henry: the temple stood in Benjamin's territory, and the tribe stayed loyal to Judah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_003.cfm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "zeal" may point to the Zealots' principles. In persecuting Christians, Paul went beyond Gamaliel's teaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the phrase "sad irony." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/philippians-3.html
- Precept Austin: "blameless" in the eyes of people, not perfect in God's eyes. Dwight Edwards notes how Paul did nothing by halves. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_34-6
- Guzik: Paul met the accepted standard of his day, which still fell short of God's standard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: these things were worse than worthless, because they kept Paul from feeling the need that drives a person to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/philippians-3.html
- Precept Austin: Paul uses bookkeeping language, with gain on one side and loss on the other. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_37-11

**v. 8**
- NET note: the word translated "rubbish" was often a crude word for dung, and probably meant to shock. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=phi&chapter=3&verse=8
- Ellicott: knowing Christ so far surpasses every other blessing that the others become "less than nothing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm
- Guzik: these things weren't worthless in themselves, only by comparison. The loss was real, not just an inner exercise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/
- Wuest (on Precept Austin): "gain Christ" means taking Christ's graces into the Christian life, not first receiving Him as Savior. Walvoord: this is personal, lived knowledge, not theory. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_37-11

**v. 9**
- Precept Austin:
  - "In Him" speaks of union with Christ, made possible because God credits Christ's righteousness to the believer.
  - "On the basis of faith" means faith is the channel, not the ground, of being declared righteous.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_39-11
- Ellicott: faith is the condition, not the source, of the gift. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm
- Gill: God credits this righteousness to His people freely, without works, like a garment put on them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/3-9.html
- Barnes: on the last day it should be found that Paul rested only on Christ's merits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/3-9.htm
- Chuck Smith: Christ took our sins and gave us His righteousness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Phl/Phl_7.cfm

**v. 10**
- Guzik lists several kinds of power in the resurrection: it proves Christ's claims, proves the cross was accepted, gives new life, and comforts us about believers who have died. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/
- Wiersbe (on Precept Austin): knowing Christ is personal, powerful, painful and practical. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_34-6
- Matthew Henry: Paul wanted to be made holy as much as he wanted to be declared righteous, with Christ's death and resurrection killing sin in him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_003.cfm
- Older commentators on biblehub: the Spirit who raised Christ raises believers now and will raise their bodies later. Paul's knowledge of Christ was real but still partial. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/3-10.htm
- Notes on the NET Bible page:
  - Paul wanted resurrection power at work in his daily life.
  - Being conformed to Christ's death means dying to his own plans for life.
  - Paul's "found in Him" echoes Christ being "found" in human likeness in chapter 2.
  
  https://netbible.org/bible/Philippians+3

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: this is the resurrection to life and glory described in vv. 20–21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm
- Matthew Henry: Paul speaks as if he could miss it, and "a holy fear of coming short" helps believers persevere. He hoped to reach it through Christ's merit, not his own. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_003.cfm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott:
  - "Attain" is a single act, and "be made perfect" is an ongoing process.
  - The picture is a runner grasping for the prize, though Paul stresses that Christ first grasped him.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm
- Guzik: Paul strove for what Jesus wanted, not for his own will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/
- Mitchell: Paul won't be perfect until he sees Christ face to face. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/3-12.html

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: the emphatic "I" sets Paul against people who thought they were already "perfect." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/philippians-3.html
- Precept Austin:
  - Quoting the Expositor's Bible Commentary, "forgetting" means refusing to let the past take over his attention, not erasing it.
  - Believers shouldn't live on past victories or be crippled by sins they have confessed.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_312-16
- Barclay: Paul will never use what he has achieved as an excuse to relax. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/philippians-3.html

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: "the heavenly calling" comes from God's will (he links Romans 8:30). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/philippians-3.html
- Quoted on Precept Austin:
  - The New American Commentary takes it as the call at the resurrection.
  - Another writer quoted there sees the prize as becoming like Christ.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_314
- Guzik: the calling is only "in Christ Jesus," unlike the legalists' efforts in their own strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/

**v. 15**
- Constable: God will make clear any smaller matters to those whose attitude is right. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/philippians-3.html
- Precept Austin:
  - One commentator thinks some were trying to reach perfection by the law.
  - MacDonald says God shows the truth to those willing to follow it.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_315-16
- Guzik: Paul wanted outside and inside pressure to push the church together, not apart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/

**v. 16**
- NET notes and Precept Austin: although perfection can't be reached in this life, the maturity already gained shouldn't be given up. https://netbible.org/bible/Philippians+3 and https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_315-16

**v. 17**
- Precept Austin: the command is "imitate me together." Paul offers himself as the model because the church had no tradition of Christian living yet. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_317-21
- Guzik: by saying "us," Paul shows he didn't see himself as the only example. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/
- NET notes name Timothy and Epaphroditus as such examples. https://netbible.org/bible/Philippians+3

**vv. 18–19**
- Ellicott sees a group here that abused freedom (the opposite of the legalists) and compares Romans 16:18. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/philippians-3.html
- Guzik: these "enemies of the cross" used freedom as an excuse for indulgence. That gave the legalists a reason to accuse Paul of "cheap grace," which is why he wept. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/
- Matthew Henry: they boasted of their sin, and if we follow their way we should fear their end. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_003.cfm
- Barnes: simply claiming to be a Christian won't save them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/philippians-3.html

**v. 20**
- Barclay and Guzik: Philippi was a Roman colony whose people never forgot Rome. In the same way, Christians are citizens of heaven living as foreigners on earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/philippians-3.html and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-3/
- Precept Austin: the Greek for "eagerly await" describes an ongoing, eager waiting. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_320-21
- The two older commentaries disagree on the word: Ellicott allows "our city" or "our citizenship," while Jamieson-Fausset-Brown prefer a different rendering. https://biblehub.com/philippians/3-20.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/philippians-3.html

**v. 21**
- Ellicott translates it "change the fashion of the body of our humiliation." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/philippians-3.html
- Precept Austin:
  - Barclay warns that "vile body" (KJV) doesn't teach the Stoic idea that the body is evil.
  - Calvin stresses God's power at work.
  - The power that can subject all things guarantees He will finish what He began.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_320-21

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 12, and vv. 12 with 15: Christian perfection.** This is the clearest divide I found.
- Calvin (Reformed): even the most devoted don't reach perfection in knowing Christ while they live. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/3-12.html
- Barnes (Presbyterian): this plainly says Paul didn't think himself free from sin. He notes the verse doesn't say no one could ever be. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/3-12.html
- Adam Clarke (Methodist) disagrees. He says Paul isn't confessing remaining sin, which he calls a false and dangerous view. "Not yet perfect" means Paul hadn't yet finished his race by dying as a martyr. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/3-12.html
- John Wesley preached his sermon "Christian Perfection" on this verse. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-40-christian-perfection/
- A Holiness book on the Wesley Center site says Paul denies perfection in v. 12 but includes himself among the "perfect" in v. 15: he was "perfect, but not perfected." https://wesley.nnu.edu/fileadmin/lib/view_wc_book.php?hdm=0641
- The Light of Israel commentary says Wesley taught perfection could be reached in this life, while he and Calvin both stressed striving toward the ideal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/3-12.html
- Gill (Baptist) takes a middle line: Paul was perfect as a new creature in all its parts and in being made right with God, but not yet in how far he had grown. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/3-12.html

**vv. 11–12: assurance and perseverance.**
- Ellicott (Anglican): Paul didn't believe in a grip on salvation that can never be lost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm
- Matthew Henry: Paul's language of possibly falling short reflects a healthy fear that helps believers persevere. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Phl/Phl_003.cfm

**v. 11: what "resurrection from the dead" means.**
- Constable (dispensationalist) thinks Paul probably means the Rapture and hoped to live to see it. https://netbible.org/bible/Philippians+3
- Ellicott: it means the resurrection to life and glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/philippians/3.htm

**v. 9: imputed righteousness.** Precept Austin, Gill, Chuck Smith and the Bible Hub study notes all say plainly that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believer. The Bible Hub sermons page quotes the Anglican Richard Hooker in the same sense. I found no sources from other traditions here to compare. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_39-11 and https://biblehub.com/sermons/philippians/3-9.htm

---

## 3. Other views

**v. 9: "faith in Christ" or "Christ's faithfulness"?**
- The NET translates "Christ's faithfulness" but its note says "a decision is difficult." It cites a grammar that calls the grammar "not decisive" and says this reading doesn't deny faith in Christ. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Phi&chapter=3&verse=9
- Against this, the Contending for the Faith commentary quotes Hawthorne in favour of "faith in Christ." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/3-9.html

**v. 3: a wording note.** The NET note reads the Greek as worship "by the Spirit," not worship of the Spirit. https://netbible.org/bible/Philippians+3
